title: Vesak, deeper
hookLine: the triple blessed day; why Theravada lands keep birth, awakening and passing on one full moon

cards: Colombo on Vesak night. Streets strung with paper lanterns. Giant lit gateways, called thoranas, telling stories from the Buddha's past lives in painted scenes and colored bulbs.
And along the roadsides, people handing out free food and drinks to anyone passing, strangers included. Those are dansal, stalls for giving. Nobody pays.
You met Vesak in your first year on this path: one full moon that holds three events, the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away. Today, deeper.

teach.b: Why one night for three events? In the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, the commentaries place all three on the full moon of the month of Vesakha, which usually falls in May.
Birth in the Lumbini garden. Awakening under the tree at Bodh Gaya, at thirty-five, tradition says. The final passing at Kusinara, at eighty.
Not every tradition counts it that way.
In much of East Asia, the three are kept on separate days: the birth in spring, the awakening in winter, the passing in early spring.
In Tibet, they're honored together in Saga Dawa, a whole lunar month, which gets its own day later in this part. Different traditions, different reckonings.
In 1950, Buddhists from many countries met in Sri Lanka and agreed to celebrate Vesak together on the full moon of May. In 1999 the United Nations recognized the Day of Vesak.
But under the lanterns, much of Vesak is quiet. People go to the temple dressed in white. They offer flowers, and a traditional verse of offering recalls that the flowers will fade.

Some keep the eight precepts for the day: the usual five, plus not eating after noon, setting aside entertainment and adornment, and not using high, luxurious beds. A whole day lived a little like a monastic.
Born, awake, gone: the festival holds a whole life, and invites one day of practice inside it.

how: On Vesak, Buddhists in Theravada countries visit temples dressed in white, offer flowers, lights and incense, listen to teachings, keep the eight precepts for the day, and give food and drink freely at roadside stalls.

games.q: it's Vesak night in Colombo. a stranger at a roadside stall hands you a drink. what do you owe?
o: nothing; it's a dansal, given freely.
games.why: dansal are stalls for giving. on Vesak, people give food and drink to anyone passing, as an act of generosity.

practice: Walk through a day of eight precepts in your mind, perhaps on the next full moon: no harm to any living thing, nothing taken that isn't given, no sexual activity, no false speech, no intoxicants, no food after noon, no entertainment or adornment, a simple bed.
Notice which one you'd find hardest, and smile at it. Then picture the day itself: quieter, simpler, roomier.

wordCard.voice: Vesak. The full moon of the month Vesakha, when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on one night. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Vesakha: the lunar month, usually April–May, whose full moon is Vesak.

carryVoice: Your line: born, awake, gone. One night holds a whole life, and a day of practice. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.41 (Uposatha Sutta), the eight precepts
